questions.text:
You are Meera/Manoj, a resident of Green Park Colony, Delhi. The park in your colony has become dirty because residents throw garbage and the municipal staff do not clean it regularly. Write a letter to the Editor of a local daily, in 100-120 words, expressing your concern and suggesting remedies.
(5 marks)
questions.answer:
Format: sender's address, date, receiver's address (The Editor, The Daily Herald, New Delhi), subject line, salutation, body in 2 paragraphs, complimentary close and name. Model answer (about 110 words):

12, Green Park Colony
New Delhi
12 March 20XX
The Editor
The Daily Herald
New Delhi
Subject: Neglected condition of the park in Green Park Colony
Sir,
Through the columns of your newspaper I wish to draw the attention of the authorities to the poor condition of the park in our colony. Residents throw plastic bags and food waste in the open and the municipal staff do not clear it regularly. The stench and mosquitoes are a health hazard for children and senior citizens who use the park.
I suggest that dustbins be placed at several points, the staff clean the park daily and residents be fined for littering. Awareness drives by the Residents' Welfare Association would also help.
Yours truly
Meera/Manoj

Marking: format 1, content 2, expression/accuracy 2.

questions.text:
Your friend Rohan/Rohini has failed in the pre-board mathematics examination and is very depressed. Write a letter, in 100-120 words, to him/her consoling him/her and advising him/her how to prepare for the final examination. Sign yourself as Aman/Anita.
(5 marks)
questions.answer:
Format: sender's address, date, salutation (Dear Rohan), informal opening, body, closing (Your loving friend) and name. Model answer (about 110 words):

25, Lake Road
Pune
5 February 20XX
Dear Rohan
I was sorry to hear that you did not do well in the maths pre-board. Please do not be depressed; this is only a practice test and it has shown you where you are weak. Many successful people have failed before they succeeded.
I suggest that you list the chapters you found hard and revise them daily for an hour. Solve previous years' papers and ask your teacher to clear your doubts. Get enough sleep and do not lose confidence. I am sure that you will do well in the finals. Write to me soon and call me if you need help.
Your loving friend
Aman/Anita

Marking: format 1, content 2, expression/accuracy 2.

questions.text:
Your school is organising a Book Fair on 20 and 21 September in the school auditorium. As the Secretary of the Literary Club, write a notice in not more than 50 words, inviting students to attend and mentioning the details.
(5 marks)
questions.answer:
Model notice (about 50 words):

St. Mary's Senior Secondary School
NOTICE
10 September 20XX
Book Fair
The Literary Club is organising a Book Fair on 20 and 21 September, 10 a.m. to 4 p.m., in the school auditorium. Books on fiction, science and general knowledge will be on sale at discount. All students are invited to attend and encouraged to bring their parents.
Secretary, Literary Club

Marking: format (heading, date, title, signature with designation) 1, content (what, when, where, who) 2, expression 2. Word limit: 50 words.

questions.text:
Write an article, in 150-200 words, on 'The Importance of Reading Habit Among Teenagers'. You are Gaurav/Gauri, a student of Class X.
(10 marks)
questions.answer:
Format: title, by-line, introduction, body in 2-3 paragraphs, conclusion. Model answer (about 170 words):

The Importance of Reading Habit Among Teenagers
By Gaurav/Gauri

In a world full of screens, reading has become a forgotten pleasure. Yet a reading habit is among the best gifts a teenager can give himself.
Books widen our knowledge and teach us about people, places and ideas that we may never meet in life. Regular reading improves vocabulary, concentration and writing skills, which help in school and in competitive examinations. Stories also build imagination and make us more sympathetic towards others, while biographies show how great people overcame difficulties.
Reading is also a healthy way to relax; it calms the mind and reduces the time spent on mobile phones and social media. Teenagers can begin by choosing subjects they enjoy, setting aside a fixed time every day and joining a school library or reading club. Parents and teachers can encourage them by gifting books and discussing what they read.
In short, a good book is a lifelong friend. Let us all make reading part of our daily routine.

Marking: format 1, content 4, fluency 2, accuracy 3.

questions.text:
Study the following graph described in words and write an analytical paragraph of 100-120 words.

A bar graph shows the percentage of students of a school using different modes of transport to reach school in the year 20XX: Walking 12%, Bicycle 18%, School bus 40%, Private car 20%, Public transport 10%.
(5 marks)
questions.answer:
Model answer (about 110 words):

The bar graph illustrates the modes of transport used by the students of a school to reach it. It is clear that the school bus is the most popular mode, used by 40 per cent of the students. The second place is held by private cars, which carry 20 per cent. Bicycles are used by 18 per cent, while 12 per cent of the students walk to school. Public transport is the least used, with only 10 per cent.
The graph shows that nearly two-thirds of the students depend on motorised transport provided by the school or their parents, and only 30 per cent use healthy, pollution-free modes such as walking and cycling. Schools could encourage cycling to reduce traffic and pollution.

Marking: introduction 1, accurate data and comparison 2, conclusion/analysis 1, language 1. Figures must be the same as in the graph.

questions.text:
Your school's annual sports day was cancelled due to heavy rain. As Sports Captain, write a formal letter, in 100-120 words, to the Principal requesting that it be rescheduled and suggesting a suitable date and arrangements. Sign yourself as Sandeep/Sandhya.
(5 marks)
questions.answer:
Format: sender's address, date, receiver (The Principal), subject, salutation (Respected Madam/Sir), body, close (Yours obediently). Model answer (about 110 words):

Sports Captain
St. Mary's School
Lucknow
18 November 20XX
The Principal
St. Mary's School
Lucknow
Subject: Request to reschedule the Annual Sports Day
Respected Madam
I regret to say that the Annual Sports Day, which was to be held on 17 November, was cancelled because of heavy rain. Students had practised for months and are very disappointed.

questions.text: What qualities of Richard Ebright as a child pointed towards his becoming a scientist? (The Making of a Scientist)
questions.answer: Richard was curious and observant. As a child he began collecting butterflies, observed them closely and kept asking questions about them. He did not give up when he met difficulties and he enjoyed finding answers by himself. This curiosity and persistence marked him out as a future scientist.

questions.text: How did Richard's parents help him develop his interests? (The Making of a Scientist)
questions.answer: His mother and father encouraged him and never discouraged his hobbies. They supplied him with books, equipment and the freedom to experiment. Their support and interest gave him the confidence to pursue his curiosity seriously.

questions.text: 'Richard did not stop at collecting butterflies.' How did his interest in butterflies grow into scientific work? (The Making of a Scientist)
questions.answer: At first Richard only collected butterflies, but he then began to study them and ask why they behaved as they did. He carried out experiments with monarch butterflies, set up a problem to solve, observed carefully and drew conclusions. This movement from collecting to investigating made him a scientist.

questions.text: The lesson says that science is not only about reading many books. In about 100-120 words, explain what, according to the lesson, a person must do to become a scientist, with reference to Richard.
questions.answer: The lesson shows that reading is only a beginning. A person who wishes to be a scientist must observe closely, ask questions and think about what he sees. He must then test his ideas by experiments and be ready to be patient and to try again after failures. Richard did exactly this: he began with collecting butterflies, wondered about their lives, designed his own experiments and recorded results carefully. Encouragement at home and from teachers helped him keep going. Thus curiosity, observation, experiment and perseverance, along with support, make a scientist.

questions.text: Write a character sketch of Richard Ebright in about 100-120 words, on the basis of the lesson.
questions.answer: Richard Ebright was an intelligent, curious and determined boy. His love for nature began with butterfly collecting, but he soon wanted to know more and began to ask questions and conduct experiments. He was hardworking and patient, and did not lose heart when the work was difficult. He used his time wisely and followed his interests seriously. He was fortunate in having parents who encouraged him, and he repaid their faith by excelling in studies and graduating with the highest honours. He is a model for young learners who wish to turn curiosity into achievement.

questions.text: Why was Sulekha called 'Bholi'? How did her appearance and speech affect the way her family treated her? (Bholi)
questions.answer: Sulekha was called Bholi, meaning simpleton, because she was a slow child who did not seem bright. She had fallen ill with smallpox, which left her face scarred, and she stammered. Her family therefore neglected her and thought her dull; her parents worried about her marriage, and her sisters were treated better.

questions.text: Why did Ramlal finally send Bholi to school? (Bholi)
questions.answer: Ramlal, the Numberdar, sent Bholi to school only because the Tehsildar had come to the village and was setting up a girls' school. Ramlal feared that if he refused he would displease the official. It was thus fear, not any concern for Bholi's education, which made him send her.

questions.text: How did the teacher's behaviour help change Bholi? (Bholi)
questions.answer: The teacher was kind and gentle. She spoke to Bholi lovingly, called her by her real name Sulekha and encouraged her to read and speak without fear. Her patience gave Bholi confidence, helped her to overcome her stammer and made her want to learn.

questions.text: Why did Bholi reject the groom at her wedding? (Bholi)
questions.answer: The groom's family demanded more dowry and showed greed, and the groom himself was an older, lame man. Bholi, who had become educated and confident, realised she was being treated like a thing to be sold, and refused to marry such a greedy man.

questions.text: Contrast Bholi before and after she went to school. (Bholi)
questions.answer: Before school Bholi was shy, frightened, neglected and unable to speak without stammering. After schooling she became confident and courageous. She could speak clearly, take a decision about her own life and stand against injustice, as she did by refusing the greedy groom.

questions.text: 'Education empowers.' In about 100-120 words, show how this is proved by the story of Bholi.
questions.answer: Bholi's story shows how education gives courage. As a child she was neglected, called a simpleton and frightened of everyone. At school her kind teacher taught her to read and to speak without fear. Slowly her stammer disappeared and her self-respect grew. When her marriage was fixed with a greedy, lame, older man, the old Bholi would have submitted, but the educated Sulekha refused and took her own decision. She even promised to look after her parents and to teach in the village school. Thus education made her independent and strong.

questions.text: Describe the wedding scene in 'Bholi' and its outcome in about 100-120 words.
questions.answer: Bholi was dressed as a bride and was frightened as the wedding party arrived. The groom's side demanded more dowry than had been settled, and the bridegroom was lame and no longer young. When Bholi was asked to garland him, she saw his greed and refused. She spoke clearly, without stammering, and said she would not marry such a man. Her father, Ramlal, was helpless and the groom's party left. Bholi then declared she would stay with her parents and serve them, and would also teach in the village school.

questions.text: Draw a character sketch of Bholi's teacher in about 100-120 words.
questions.answer: Bholi's teacher was a gentle, understanding and patient woman. When Bholi first came to school, frightened and stammering, the teacher did not scold her but welcomed her with affection. She addressed her as Sulekha, giving her an identity and self-respect. She made her read and write and told her not to be afraid. She trusted that the child could learn, and by her care she transformed a timid girl into a confident one. She is an example of how a teacher's love can change a student's life.

questions.text: The Tehsildar's visit changed the course of Bholi's life. Explain how, in about 100-120 words.
questions.answer: The Tehsildar, a government official, visited the village and opened a school for girls. Ramlal, fearing he would be displeased, enrolled Bholi even though he cared little for her education. This chance, which came out of fear, took Bholi into a place where she met a kind teacher. She learnt to read, write and speak confidently, and she gained self-respect. Years later, when her marriage was arranged with a greedy man, she refused. Thus the Tehsildar's visit indirectly gave Bholi the education and courage to shape her own life.

questions.text: What does Bholi's decision at the end say about her character? (Bholi)
questions.answer: Her decision shows that she has become brave, confident and self-respecting. She refuses a greedy groom, speaks without stammering and promises to look after her parents and to teach. She values her dignity above social pressure.

questions.text: Why did the Martians come to Earth, and why did they finally go back? (The Book That Saved the Earth)
questions.answer: The Martians, led by Think-Tank, came to invade and conquer Earth. They found a book of nursery rhymes, wrongly took it for a source of Earth's scientific knowledge and thought Earthlings were powerful and dangerous. Frightened, they called off the invasion and returned to Mars.

questions.text: How did the Martians misinterpret the rhyme 'Hey Diddle Diddle'? (The Book That Saved the Earth)
questions.answer: The rhyme speaks of a cow jumping over the moon, a cat playing the fiddle and a dish running away with the spoon. The Martians took these as facts and concluded that Earth's cows could leap to the moon and that Earthlings had great powers and strange weapons.

questions.text: How does the play show the Martians' foolishness? (The Book That Saved the Earth)
questions.answer: The Martians relied on their machines and logical reasoning but lacked common sense. They failed to see that the book was only a collection of nursery rhymes and read them literally. Their serious misreading of simple rhymes makes them comic and shows their arrogance.

questions.text: What is the role of Think-Tank in the play? (The Book That Saved the Earth)
questions.answer: Think-Tank is the Martian chief who commands the invasion and takes decisions. He is proud and confident of Martian superiority, yet he accepts the wrong interpretation of the book and orders a retreat, showing his foolishness.
questions.basis: The Book That Saved the Earth: character question

questions.text: 'The play is both humorous and a lesson on the importance of books.' Explain. (The Book That Saved the Earth)
questions.answer: The humour lies in the Martians taking nursery rhymes literally and getting frightened. The lesson is that a book, even a simple one, saved the Earth from invasion, and that knowledge and its right understanding are powerful.

questions.text: Describe how the Martians interpreted the book and what they decided, in about 100-120 words.
questions.answer: The Martians came across a book of Earth's nursery rhymes. Not understanding what it was, they treated it as a record of Earth's science and power. Rhymes such as 'Hey Diddle Diddle' made them believe cows could jump over the moon, and 'Humpty Dumpty' seemed to hint at a mighty force that could not be defeated. They concluded that Earthlings were highly advanced and dangerous. Think-Tank decided that attacking was too risky, so they called off the invasion and sailed back to Mars.

questions.text: Do you think the title 'The Book That Saved the Earth' is appropriate? Give reasons in about 100-120 words.
questions.answer: The title is appropriate because a single book decided Earth's fate. The Martians had come armed with advanced technology to conquer the planet, but they discovered a book of nursery rhymes. Misreading it, they thought Earthlings had amazing abilities and strange weapons, and gave up their attack. The title also has a humorous irony, as the book that saved Earth was only a children's collection and not a weapon. It also points out the power of books and ideas, which can achieve what armies sometimes cannot.

questions.text: The play warns against taking things literally and drawing conclusions without proper knowledge. Justify, in about 100-120 words.
questions.answer: The Martians took 'Hey Diddle Diddle' and other rhymes literally and concluded that cows jump over the moon and that Earthlings possess incredible powers. Because they lacked knowledge of Earth's culture, they reached a wrong conclusion and abandoned their invasion. The play thus warns that incomplete knowledge and hasty reading can lead to foolish decisions. It also suggests that proud, machine-dependent people may overlook plain common sense. Understanding context, and asking before concluding, is the lesson.

questions.text: What does the play suggest about the importance of books in our lives? (The Book That Saved the Earth)
questions.answer: The play shows that even a simple book can have great power; it saved the Earth by its mere existence. Books preserve the knowledge and culture of a people, and a book's meaning can protect or mislead depending on how it is read. We should read and value books.

questions.text: Why do you think the author chose a nursery-rhyme book for the plot? (The Book That Saved the Earth)
questions.answer: A nursery-rhyme book is simple and well known to every child, so its misinterpretation by the Martians is both funny and surprising. It makes the contrast between powerful but foolish invaders and a harmless book very clear, creating humour and a message.

questions.text: What is the central idea of the poem 'Dust of Snow'?
questions.answer: The poem shows how a small, unexpected incident in nature can change a person's mood. The poet, who was sad and regretting his day, is touched when a crow shakes snow on him. His gloom lifts, and the poem tells us that nature, even in its humblest forms, can heal and bring joy.

questions.text: Why has the poet chosen a crow and a hemlock tree rather than a bird and tree that are usually thought pleasant? (Dust of Snow)
questions.answer: The crow is a bird people regard as a bad omen, and the hemlock is a poisonous tree. By choosing these, the poet shows that even things seen as gloomy or harmful can bring joy. The change of mood thus comes from the least expected source, which gives the poem its irony.

questions.text: What does 'a change of mood' mean in the poem? How was the poet's mood before and after the incident? (Dust of Snow)
questions.answer: A change of mood means a shift from one feeling to another. Before the incident the poet was sad and regretted the way the day was going. After the dust of snow fell on him, he felt cheered and his heart was relieved, so a part of the day was saved from being wasted.

questions.text: Explain the line 'And saved some part / Of a day I had rued.' (Dust of Snow)
questions.answer: The poet had been regretting his day, thinking it was wasted. The simple touch of snow from the crow lifted his spirits and the rest of the day became better. 'Saved' shows that the incident rescued some part of the day from being spent in sorrow.

questions.text: What is the figure of speech or poetic device in the line 'The way a crow / Shook down on me'? Explain. (Dust of Snow)
questions.answer: The crow is described as shaking down snow as if it does so purposely, giving it a human-like action; the effect of the line is to make nature appear to take a friendly interest in the poet. The words 'dust of snow' and 'hemlock tree' also create a vivid, wintry image.

questions.text: What lesson does the poem teach us about nature and our moods? (Dust of Snow)
questions.answer: The poem teaches that nature has the power to heal and refresh us. We need not look for big events to be happy; a small incident, noticed with an open mind, can lift gloom. It encourages us to be sensitive to the beauty and surprises of the natural world.

questions.text: The poem is only eight lines long, yet it has a strong impact. How is this achieved? (Dust of Snow)
questions.answer: The poem uses simple words and a single clear incident, the crow shaking down snow. Its rhyme scheme, short lines and brief but vivid images (dust of snow, hemlock tree) keep it compact. The sudden change from regret to joy in the last four lines gives it emotional force.

questions.text: Describe the setting of the poem and its mood. (Dust of Snow)
questions.answer: The setting is a snowy winter day, where a crow sits on a hemlock tree and shakes some snow down on the poet. At first the mood is one of regret and sadness; by the end it is light and cheerful, as the poet's heart is given a change of mood.

questions.text: 'The poet was not looking for happiness, yet he found it.' Explain with reference to the poem. (Dust of Snow)
questions.answer: The poet was in a gloomy mood, feeling the day was wasted, and was not expecting anything to cheer him. The crow suddenly shook snow down upon him, and this simple act changed his feelings. The poem suggests that joy often comes unexpectedly from small natural things.

questions.text: What is the central idea of the poem 'Fire and Ice'?
questions.answer: Through the question of how the world will end, the poet explains that human emotions can be as destructive as fire and ice. Fire stands for desire and greed, and ice for hatred. Either of them is powerful enough to destroy the world, so we must control our feelings.

questions.text: What does fire symbolise in the poem, and why does the poet favour it? (Fire and Ice)
questions.answer: Fire symbolises desire, which includes greed, passion and craving. The poet says that from what he has tasted of desire he holds with those who favour fire, as he knows its power to consume people and the world through his own experience.

questions.text: What does ice stand for in the poem? Why is it equally capable of destroying the world? (Fire and Ice)
questions.answer: Ice stands for hatred and cold, unfeeling indifference. It shows that hatred can freeze relationships and kindness. The poet says that ice would also suffice to destroy the world, as hatred is great and strong enough.

questions.text: How does the poet use the idea of 'the end of the world'? Is the tone serious or humorous? (Fire and Ice)
questions.answer: The poet begins with the common debate about whether the world will end in fire or in ice. The tone is calm and conversational, and the poet seems almost casual, but the message is serious: our own destructive feelings can bring the end of the world.

questions.text: The poem has a particular rhyme scheme. Identify it and explain how it helps the poem. (Fire and Ice)
questions.answer: The poem has a pattern of abaabcbcb, where lines rhyme irregularly, which makes it sound like a brief, thoughtful speech. The short lines, the repeated words and the neat rhyme give a feeling of completeness and make the idea easy to remember.

questions.text: Explain 'Some say the world will end in fire, / Some say in ice.' (Fire and Ice)
questions.answer: The poet refers to two views people hold about how the world will end: some think it will be destroyed by fire, others by ice. These are used as symbols of desire and hatred, so the lines are a prelude to the main idea of the poem.

questions.text: What is the figure of speech in 'Fire' and 'Ice' as they are used in the poem? (Fire and Ice)
questions.answer: Fire and ice are used as metaphors or symbols. Fire represents the burning desire and passion, and ice represents cold hatred. This symbolism turns physical forces into human emotions, giving the poem depth.

questions.text: What warning does the poet give to human beings? (Fire and Ice)
questions.answer: The poet warns that uncontrolled desire and hatred can destroy the world. Either can end life on Earth, so people must restrain their greed and hatred and live with love and sympathy.

questions.text: Why does the poet say 'I think I know enough of hate / To say that for destruction ice / Is also great / And would suffice'? (Fire and Ice)
questions.answer: The poet means that he has seen enough of hatred to know that it too is a destructive force. Cold, unfeeling hatred can ruin lives and societies as completely as fire. Hence it is equally capable of ending the world.

questions.text: What is the central idea of the poem 'A Tiger in the Zoo'?
questions.answer: The poem contrasts the tiger's life in a cage with the freedom of his natural habitat. The poet shows the tiger's strength, anger and sadness as he walks within bars, while he should be hunting in the jungle. It is a protest against keeping wild animals in captivity.

questions.text: How does the poet describe the tiger in the zoo? What is his state of mind? (A Tiger in the Zoo)
questions.answer: The tiger has vivid stripes and walks the few steps of his cage on soft pads. He seems quiet, but is full of rage inside. He ignores visitors and stares at the stars with brilliant eyes, showing his anger and longing for freedom.

questions.text: What does the tiger do in his cage, and what should he be doing in the wild according to the poet? (A Tiger in the Zoo)
questions.answer: In the cage he stalks the few steps, ignoring visitors and the patrolling cars. In the wild he should be lurking in the shadow, sliding through the long grass near the water hole where plump deer pass, snarling around houses and terrorising the village.

questions.text: What is the 'quiet rage' of the tiger? Why is it quiet? (A Tiger in the Zoo)
questions.answer: The tiger is angry at being locked up and denied the life he deserves. His rage is quiet because he cannot show it by roaring or attacking: he is caged, powerless and can only pace silently on soft pads. It is a suppressed, helpless anger.

questions.text: How do the two contrasting pictures of the tiger in the poem heighten the poet's message? (A Tiger in the Zoo)
questions.answer: One picture shows the tiger free and fierce in the forest, sliding through grass and terrorising the village; the other shows him in a concrete cell with his strength behind bars. The contrast makes us feel the cruelty of captivity and the waste of the animal's power.

questions.text: What is the effect of the phrase 'on pads of velvet quiet'? (A Tiger in the Zoo)
questions.answer: The tiger's soft paws are described as pads of velvet, which creates an image of silence and smoothness. It shows his stealth and strength held in check, and it contrasts with the roar one might expect from a tiger.

questions.text: Comment on the poet's attitude to the 'patrolling cars' and the visitors in the poem. (A Tiger in the Zoo)
questions.answer: The tiger ignores visitors and the sound of cars, which shows his contempt for those who watch him in captivity. The poet suggests that he is far above such small matters, as his mind is on the wild and the stars he longs for.

questions.text: What does the poem suggest about the place of wild animals in society? (A Tiger in the Zoo)
questions.answer: The poem suggests that wild animals belong in the forest, not in zoos or cages. Keeping them locked up makes them suffer and robs them of their natural life. We should respect their freedom and protect their habitats.

questions.text: Why does the tiger stare at the stars at night? (A Tiger in the Zoo)
questions.answer: At night the tiger hears the patrolling cars and the last voices and stares at the brilliant stars with his brilliant eyes. He may be longing for freedom and the open night sky of the jungle, which he should be roaming. The stars show his dream of a free life.

questions.text: How does the poet help us to tell a Bengal tiger from other animals? (How to Tell Wild Animals)
questions.answer: The poet says that if a noble wild beast with black stripes on a yellow ground greets you, you should just notice whether he eats you. The humorous 'test' is that if he does, he is the Bengal tiger. The poet thus teaches recognition in a comic way.

questions.text: How can we tell a crocodile from a hyena, according to the poem? (How to Tell Wild Animals)
questions.answer: The poet says a novice may find it hard to tell them apart, but a hyena comes with a merry smile, as the hyena is said to laugh. If the animal is weeping, it is a crocodile, because crocodiles are known for 'crocodile tears'.

questions.text: What is the tone of the poem 'How to Tell Wild Animals'? How is humour created? (How to Tell Wild Animals)
questions.answer: The tone is light, humorous and mock-serious. Humour is created by giving absurd 'identification tests' which one could only use after meeting danger, such as recognising the tiger by whether he eats you. The jolly rhymes add to the fun.

questions.text: What does the poet mean by 'a novice' in the poem and why is advice given to him? (How to Tell Wild Animals)
questions.answer: A novice is a beginner with no experience of wild animals. The poet gives advice to him, humorously, on how to identify various beasts of prey. It is a comic guide for a person who may meet these animals, though the advice is impractical.

questions.text: What is the central idea of 'The Ball Poem'?
questions.answer: A boy loses his ball and cries; the poet tells us that the boy is learning about loss and responsibility. A ball can be replaced by money but the lesson of loss cannot. The poem shows how a small incident teaches a child to accept loss and to grow up.

questions.text: Why does the poet not offer the boy money or a new ball? (The Ball Poem)
questions.answer: The poet knows that a replacement would not teach the boy the lesson of loss. A new ball cannot take the place of the lost one, and the boy must learn to bear his loss himself. So the poet does not intrude on him and respects his grief.

questions.text: What does the poet mean by 'the epistemology of loss'? (The Ball Poem)
questions.answer: Epistemology means the study of knowledge. The poet means that the boy is learning, by experience, what loss is and how to cope with it. The lesson of his ball's loss is his first knowledge of loss and of how to stand up after it.

questions.text: 'Money is external.' What does the poet mean by this? (The Ball Poem)
questions.answer: The poet means that money cannot make up for a real loss, as it is outside the self. It can buy another ball but cannot give the boy the inner strength to handle loss. True growth comes from within and not from outside things.

questions.text: What does the poet mean by 'a world of possessions' and the boy's 'first responsibility'? (The Ball Poem)
questions.answer: The world is full of things people own and lose. The boy is beginning to realise this, and that he must be responsible for what he has. Losing his ball is his first lesson in responsibility, because he learns to value what he owns and to bear the consequences.

questions.text: Describe the boy's reaction to the loss of his ball. (The Ball Poem)
questions.answer: The boy stands by the harbour looking at the water where the ball has rolled. He is staring, hardly seeing toys any more, and is very upset. His desperate eyes show his sadness, and he is learning to stand up after the loss.

questions.text: How does the poem show the poet's sympathy for the boy? (The Ball Poem)
questions.answer: The poet understands the boy's sorrow and pity him. He does not interfere or offer easy comfort, but watches quietly, respecting the boy's need to deal with his loss by himself. His thoughtful language shows his sympathy and wisdom.

questions.text: What does the poet mean by 'how to stand up'? Why is it repeated? (The Ball Poem)
questions.answer: 'How to stand up' means how to face loss and go on with courage. The phrase is repeated to stress its importance: everyone has to learn it, and it is the main lesson of the boy's experience. It also adds a rhythm of emphasis to the poem.

questions.text: What poetic devices has the poet used in the poem? Give examples. (The Ball Poem)
questions.answer: The poem uses repetition ('What, what is he to do?', 'how to stand up'), metaphor ('the epistemology of loss'), and enjambment which carries thought from one line to the next. It also uses imagery of the boy's desperate eyes. These make the poem emotional and thoughtful.

questions.text: What is the central idea of the poem 'Amanda'?
questions.answer: The poem shows a child, Amanda, being constantly told what to do by adults, while she dreams of freedom. It brings out the child's longing to be free from criticism and orders, and it suggests that adults should respect a child's need for freedom and imagination.

questions.text: How does the poem show that Amanda is constantly scolded? (Amanda)
questions.answer: Each stanza begins with an instruction in brackets or quotes: don't bite your nails, don't hunch your shoulders, stop slouching and sit up straight. The repetition of 'Amanda!' in every command shows that the adult keeps scolding her about every small habit.

questions.text: What does Amanda imagine herself to be? What does it show about her wishes? (Amanda)
questions.answer: Amanda imagines herself as a mermaid drifting blissfully in a languid, emerald sea, and also as free and alone like an orphan, with no one to order her. It shows she longs for freedom, peace and a world of her own, away from rules.

questions.text: What is the difference between the voices in the brackets and those outside in the poem? (Amanda)
questions.answer: The voices outside the brackets are the adult's commands, scolding Amanda. The voices within brackets are Amanda's own dreams and thoughts. The contrast shows the gap between the adult world of demands and the child's world of imagination.

questions.text: How is Amanda's mermaid dream different from her actual condition? (Amanda)
questions.answer: As a mermaid she is the sole inhabitant of a calm, languid sea, drifting blissfully with no one to command her. In real life she is surrounded by orders and criticism. The dream is an escape from reality.

questions.text: What is the tone of the poem? Is it serious or humorous? (Amanda)
questions.answer: The tone is gently humorous but with a touch of sympathy for the child. The scolding is exaggerated and amusing, but behind the humour there is a serious point about children's lack of freedom.

questions.text: Which poetic devices are used in the poem 'Amanda'? Give examples. (Amanda)
questions.answer: Repetition of the name 'Amanda' stresses the constant scolding; the imperative sentences ('Don't bite your nails') show commands; the mermaid is a metaphor of freedom; and 'languid, emerald sea' is a visual image. Together they create contrast between adults and the child.

questions.text: What lesson does the poem give to parents and elders? (Amanda)
questions.answer: The poem tells elders not to nag children about every small thing. Children need freedom to be themselves and to dream. Constant criticism may harm their confidence, so elders should guide with understanding and love.

questions.text: 'Don't bite your nails, Amanda!' What do such instructions show about the speaker? (Amanda)
questions.answer: They show that the speaker is a controlling adult who cares about good habits but is overbearing. She corrects Amanda's posture and habits without giving her any space, so her care appears like nagging.

questions.text: What is the central idea of the poem 'The Trees'?
questions.answer: The poem presents trees as living beings that long to return to the forest, their natural home. It shows how people confine nature by making it a part of houses and cities, and suggests that nature will reclaim its freedom. It is also about the need for a free life.

questions.text: What is meant by 'The trees inside are moving out into the forest'? (The Trees)
questions.answer: The poet imagines the trees that have been kept inside the house as moving out into the forest where they belong. Literally, the wood of the house is made from trees; metaphorically, they are returning to their natural home in the forest after being confined.

questions.text: How is the forest described in the poem before the trees arrive? (The Trees)
questions.answer: The forest is described as empty all these days, with no bird to sit, no insect to hide and no sun to bury its feet in the shadow. The forest was waiting for the trees, which shows how essential they are to it.

questions.text: What does the poet do while the trees depart? What does it show about her attitude? (The Trees)
questions.answer: The poet sits inside, doors open to the veranda, writing long letters in which she scarcely mentions the departure of the forest from the house. She does not stop them or complain, which suggests that she accepts and even welcomes their freedom.

questions.text: Which poetic devices does the poet use in 'The Trees'? (The Trees)
questions.answer: The main device is personification, since trees are shown as living things which move, work and strain. There are also similes ('like newly discharged patients') and imagery. These devices make the trees seem alive and eager to be free.

questions.text: Why does the poet say the 'house' is a place of confinement for the trees? (The Trees)
questions.answer: The roots work to disengage themselves from the cracks in the veranda floor and the leaves strain toward the glass. This shows that the house keeps the trees imprisoned, and that they are struggling to get out into open nature.

questions.text: What is the central idea of the poem 'Fog'?
questions.answer: The poem is a short description of fog as a quiet cat. Like a cat, the fog comes silently, sits and looks over the harbour and the city, and then moves on. It shows the soft, gentle and mysterious nature of fog through a single extended metaphor.

questions.text: Which metaphor does the poet use in 'Fog' and how is it appropriate? (Fog)
questions.answer: The poet compares fog to a cat: it comes on little cat feet, sits on silent haunches and then moves on. Fog arrives noiselessly, settles over a place and leaves, as a cat does, so the comparison is natural and effective.

questions.text: What does 'on silent haunches' suggest about the fog? (Fog)
questions.answer: Haunches are the hind legs of an animal, and a cat sits on them. 'Silent haunches' shows that fog sits quietly and still above the harbour and city. It gives the fog the look of a watchful, patient cat.

questions.text: Where does the fog sit and what does it do? (Fog)
questions.answer: The fog sits looking over the harbour and the city. It watches them quietly for some time, covering them, and then moves on. It is shown as an observer which does no harm and leaves without disturbance.

questions.text: Why is the poem called 'Fog'? What is the effect of its brevity? (Fog)
questions.answer: The poem is about fog, and everything in it, the cat comparison, the quiet movement and its sudden departure, describes it. The brevity of six lines matches the short stay of fog, and gives it the same light, passing feel.

questions.text: What is the mood of the poem? How is it created? (Fog)
questions.answer: The mood is quiet, calm and mysterious. It is created by soft words like 'little cat feet' and 'silent haunches', short lines and a gentle rhythm, which make the reader feel the hush of the fog.

questions.text: What does the poem tell us about the nature of fog? (Fog)
questions.answer: It tells us that the fog comes in suddenly and quietly, stays for a while covering everything and then goes away without any trace. It is gentle and harmless, yet it dominates its surroundings for a short while.

questions.text: The poem uses very few words. Why is it still effective? (Fog)
questions.answer: A single clear image is developed throughout, the cat. Each phrase adds to the image: arrival, sitting, watching, leaving. The simple words, rhythm and imagery produce a vivid picture of fog in few lines.

questions.text: Describe how the poet gives fog the qualities of a cat. (Fog)
questions.answer: The fog comes on 'little cat feet', that is, silently; it sits on 'silent haunches' like a cat resting; it looks over the harbour and city as a cat observes its surroundings; and then it moves on as a cat wanders off. The images give fog animal qualities.

questions.text: What is the central idea of 'The Tale of Custard the Dragon'?
questions.answer: The poem is a humorous ballad about Custard, a dragon who is thought a coward by everyone because he cries for a nice safe cage, but who proves to be the only one who saves Belinda by killing the pirate. It tells us that real courage is shown in time of danger, not by boasting.

questions.text: Who are Belinda's pets and what are they like? (The Tale of Custard the Dragon)
questions.answer: Belinda lives with a little black kitten called Ink, a little grey mouse called Blink, a little yellow dog called Mustard and a realio, trulio, little pet dragon called Custard. All except Custard are called brave: Ink and Blink chase lions down the stairs and Mustard is as brave as a tiger in a rage.

questions.text: Why was Custard considered a coward? How did the others treat him? (The Tale of Custard the Dragon)
questions.answer: Custard cried for a nice safe cage while the others were brave. Everyone made fun of him, calling him a coward. Belinda tickled him unmercifully and the others rudely called him Percival, so he was laughed at in the house.

questions.text: How did the other pets behave when the pirate came? How did Custard behave? (The Tale of Custard the Dragon)
questions.answer: When the pirate came, Ink and Blink ran under the bed and Mustard growled and ran away, so the supposedly brave pets deserted Belinda. Custard, the 'coward', snorted and gobbled the pirate, saving Belinda.

questions.text: Explain the irony in the poem. (The Tale of Custard the Dragon)
questions.answer: The animals who boasted of their courage ran away when the danger came, while the dragon, ridiculed as a coward, was the only one to fight and save Belinda. After the victory he is still the same, crying for a nice safe cage, which adds to the irony.

questions.text: How does the poet create humour in the poem? (The Tale of Custard the Dragon)
questions.answer: Humour comes from the made-up words 'realio, trulio', the comic names such as Ink, Blink and Mustard, exaggerated similes like 'as brave as a barrelful of bears', and the contrast between the fierce-looking dragon and his cowardice.

questions.text: Describe Custard's appearance as given in the poem. (The Tale of Custard the Dragon)
questions.answer: Custard has big sharp teeth, spikes on top and scales underneath. His mouth is like a fireplace, his nose like a chimney and he has 'realio, trulio' daggers on his toes. His fearsome appearance makes his cowardice funnier.

questions.text: Which poetic devices have been used in the poem? Give examples. (The Tale of Custard the Dragon)
questions.answer: Similes: 'as brave as a barrelful of bears' and 'as brave as a tiger in a rage'; metaphor: 'mouth like a fireplace'; repetition: 'realio, trulio'; and rhyme in couplets (Ink and Blink, Mustard and Custard). These give it a lively sing-song quality.

questions.text: What does the end of the poem tell us about Custard? (The Tale of Custard the Dragon)
questions.answer: The ending shows that Belinda is still as brave as a barrelful of bears, Ink and Blink chase lions, Mustard is brave as a tiger, but Custard keeps crying for a nice safe cage. Though he saved Belinda, he remains the same; the poem ends humorously, with nothing changed.

questions.text: What is the central idea of the poem 'For Anne Gregory'?
questions.answer: The poem says that a person should be loved for what she is and not for her physical appearance. A young man may love Anne for her yellow hair, but the poet wishes that she be loved for herself alone, and finally says only God can love a person for herself alone.

questions.text: Why can no young man love Anne 'for yourself alone'? (For Anne Gregory)
questions.answer: The young men are attracted by her beautiful honey-coloured, yellow hair, which is her outward charm. Her beauty is so striking that men are drawn to it, so none can see and love her true self apart from her looks.

questions.text: What does Anne say she will do to test whether she can be loved for herself? (For Anne Gregory)
questions.answer: Anne says she can get a hair-dye and set a colour such as brown, black or carrot upon her hair, so that young men may love her for herself alone and not for her yellow hair. It shows that she wants to be loved for her true self.

questions.text: What did the 'old religious man' say? (For Anne Gregory)
questions.answer: He said he had found a text to prove that only God can love a person for herself alone and not for her yellow hair. It suggests that human love depends on outward things, while only God's love is pure and unconditional.

questions.text: What is the tone of the poem? Is it serious or light-hearted? (For Anne Gregory)
questions.answer: The tone is conversational and witty, as the poet speaks to Anne and she answers him playfully. Beneath the light tone there is a serious thought about love, beauty and acceptance.

questions.text: What do the 'great honey-coloured ramparts at your ear' stand for? (For Anne Gregory)
questions.answer: They stand for Anne's thick, golden-yellow hair, which falls like walls on either side of her ear. The metaphor of ramparts (walls of a fort) shows that her hair is so striking that it shields her real self from the view of young men.

questions.text: Which poetic devices are used in the poem? (For Anne Gregory)
questions.answer: The poem has metaphor ('honey-coloured ramparts'), repetition of 'for yourself alone / And not your yellow hair' as a refrain, and rhyme. Its colour imagery of yellow, brown, black and carrot makes it vivid.

questions.text: What does the poem tell us about physical beauty and real love? (For Anne Gregory)
questions.answer: The poem tells us that beauty attracts but real love should be based on a person's character and true self. Looks can be changed, as with hair-dye, and cannot be the basis for love. It teaches us to look beyond appearances.

questions.text: Anne is told that she is loved for her hair and she wishes to change it. What does this reveal about her character? (For Anne Gregory)
questions.answer: It shows that Anne is sensible and wishes to be valued for what she is, not for her appearance. She is willing to change her hair colour to test the love of young men, which shows her independent spirit and desire for sincere love.
